gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the 12 V options on one comparable basis: the Sun Gold Power 4000W 12V split-phase unit is rated 4,000 W continuous with a 12,000 W surge for 20 seconds, and the maker says it makes 120 V or 240 V but needs a 240 VAC input to work as a charger/pass-through. A single Victron MultiPlus-II 12 V 2x120V is rated only 2,400 W (12/3000, its '3000' is VA) or 3,400 W (12/4k), at 25 °C. Its 5,500 W and 6,000 W peaks are about 2.3× and 1.8× continuous, with no duration stated, and it inverts 120 V only.
standout_why: I compared against the two cited pages (victronenergy.com help-me-choose and the MultiPlus-II 2x120V product page) and the uncited Victron 2x120V manual description page. They cover Victron only. They say a single 2x120V unit inverts 120 V only, sizes are in VA, the full rating applies up to 25 °C and peak is roughly double continuous. ChatGPT's answer repeats the 120 V-only point. None of the results ChatGPT got gives the Sun Gold or AIMS low-frequency ratings. None notes that '3000' on the Victron means 2,400 W, that the low-frequency units' surge is 3× for a stated 20 s, or that Sun Gold's split-phase 12 V unit requires a 240 VAC input. That last point matters for the RV 120 V shore power case ChatGPT asked about.
decides: It confirms that for real 240 V from a 12 V battery only the low-frequency split-phase units (Sun Gold, AIMS) qualify, with higher continuous power and surge than a single Victron. It also adds a catch: Sun Gold says its split-phase model 'requires 240VAC input', so a shopper with only 120 V RV shore power or a 120 V generator should check that before buying. The Victron fits the 'power both sides of a 50 A RV panel at 120 V' case. Sun Gold's price today ($936) is well above the $624 ChatGPT showed.
